title: Kelp forest recovery from urchin barrens
bottleneck: Marine heatwaves and predator loss have flipped vast kelp forests into urchin barrens — grazed wastelands that persist for decades because urchins survive starvation and prevent kelp recruitment. Removing urchins at scale is labor-intensive and the urchin fishery economics rarely work; reseeding kelp fails when barrens persist. Whether lost forests can recover under continued warming, or the shift is permanent, is unknown.
why_it_blocks: Kelp forests rival tropical forests in productivity and support major fisheries; their collapse removes coastal protection and carbon cycling along temperate shores. The barren state may be an alternate stable state — effectively irreversible without intervention nobody knows how to do at scale.
current_state: Urchin culling programs and kelp reseeding show local successes, and sea otter recovery demonstrates predator restoration works where it happens. But heatwave-driven collapses from California to Tasmania keep outpacing recovery efforts.
